summary: Communications Equipment has become an AI-networking story with a flat telecom backdrop. Cisco booked $9.3 billion of hyperscale AI orders in fiscal 2026, about 4.5 times the prior year [2], and Arista's third-quarter revenue grew 58.5% to $3.66 billion [3]. Ciena and Nokia report optical and IP growth tied to cloud builders [5][8], while Ericsson calls the mobile RAN market flat [9]. Dell'Oro expects supply, not demand, to constrain AI switching for one to two years [10]. Component costs are weighing on margins at Arista and Ericsson [4][9]. Sub-industry consensus and forward multiples were not available to us; Damodaran's January 2026 data is the multiple reference [14].

watch: Whether hyperscaler capex keeps rising into 2027: Alphabet and Amazon both signalled higher spending, while Meta's budget is unset [12].
Supply limits: Dell'Oro expects AI switching to stay supply-constrained for at least one to two years, so shipments, not orders, may set the pace [10].
Gross-margin pressure from mix and component costs, visible at Arista (64.0% vs 65.2%), and Ericsson, which flags 2027 [3][9].
Cisco's fiscal 2027 guide of $72.2-73.4 billion revenue and whether hyperscale AI orders, $4 billion in the July quarter, keep climbing [1][2].
Customer concentration at the optical and switching names: two customers were 41.7% of Ciena's revenue [5], and Arista depends on large cloud operators [4].

basics.intro: These companies build the equipment that moves data: routers and switches in offices and data centres, optical gear that carries traffic over long distances, Wi-Fi access points, and the radio and core equipment telecom operators use for mobile networks. GICS also puts two-way radios and public-safety communications here, as with Motorola Solutions. Customers are telecom carriers, cloud giants and enterprises. Revenue comes from hardware, software and recurring support. Handsets and servers sit in Technology Hardware, Storage and Peripherals, and chips sit in Semiconductors.

products.name: Data-centre switching and routing
products.what: High-speed Ethernet switches and routers that connect servers and AI accelerators inside and between data centres. Speeds are quoted in gigabits per second.
products.examples: Arista Etherlink and EOS, Cisco Silicon One systems, Nokia IP Networks

products.name: Campus networking and Wi-Fi
products.what: Switches and wireless access points that connect offices, schools and homes, usually managed through cloud software.
products.examples: Cisco Catalyst and Meraki, HPE Aruba and Juniper Mist, Ubiquiti UniFi

products.name: Optical transport and optics
products.what: Gear that sends light signals across fibre between cities and data centres, plus pluggable optical modules that fit into switches.
products.examples: Ciena WaveLogic, Nokia Optical Networks, Cisco coherent optics

products.name: Mobile network equipment
products.what: Radios, antennas and core software that let carriers run 4G and 5G networks. Sales follow carrier spending cycles.

products.name: Mission-critical communications
products.what: Two-way radios, emergency-dispatch networks, video security and related software sold to police, fire services and governments.
products.examples: Motorola Solutions radios, body cameras and command-centre software

products.name: Software, security and support
products.what: Subscriptions, security products and support contracts sold on top of the hardware, which smooth out lumpy hardware sales.
products.examples: Cisco Security and Splunk, Arista CloudVision, Motorola Software and Services

terms.meaning: A very large cloud operator such as Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet or Meta. Its orders are large and uneven, so a few customers can move a vendor's results.
The network that links AI accelerators to each other inside a training cluster. Front-end networks connect servers to users and storage.
Ways of linking AI chips: scale-up inside a rack, scale-out across racks in a building, scale-across between buildings. Each needs different switches or optics.
Two networking standards for AI clusters. Ethernet is open and sold by many vendors; InfiniBand is mainly Nvidia's.
Switch chips sold by outside chip makers rather than designed in-house. Vendors using it compete on software and system design.
Technology that packs more data into each fibre by encoding it on the light wave. It lets operators carry more traffic over existing fibre.
Radio access network: the towers, radios and baseband equipment that connect phones to a carrier. It is the core of Ericsson's and Nokia's mobile business.
Contracted but not yet recognised revenue. Remaining performance obligations (RPO) is the accounting version. It shows visibility but not margin.
Cash received for products or services not yet delivered or recognised, often from multi-year deals. Arista's deferred revenue is watched as a sign of AI demand.
Operating margin excluding items such as stock compensation and acquisition costs. Companies here report it prominently, so compare with GAAP.
Stock held by distributors and resellers. Cisco and others sell through two tiers of channel, so shifts in that stock can distort end-demand.
A customer choosing a vendor's product for a future build. Revenue arrives months or years later as the customer deploys.

drivers.name: Cloud and AI capex
drivers.how: Hyperscalers' spending on data centres turns into orders for switches, routers and optics within quarters. Raised spending guidance lifts order books; paused projects delay shipments.

drivers.name: Carrier spending cycles
drivers.how: Telecom operators buy radio and optical gear in waves tied to 5G build-outs and network upgrades. Mobile equipment revenue is flat when carriers hold back budgets.

drivers.name: Enterprise refresh
drivers.how: Companies replace Wi-Fi and campus switches on multi-year cycles, with new standards such as Wi-Fi 7 acting as triggers. It supports steady orders and software attach.

drivers.name: Component costs and supply
drivers.how: Memory, switch chips and optical parts are bought in. When they rise or run short, vendors either raise prices or accept lower gross margin, and shipments can lag orders.

drivers.name: Product mix
drivers.how: Systems sold to hyperscalers often carry lower gross margins than campus or software products, so faster AI growth can dilute margins even as profit dollars rise.

drivers.name: Public-sector budgets
drivers.how: Government and public-safety customers buy on multi-year budgets and long contracts. This gives Motorola Solutions a backlog that moves slowly.

business: Revenue comes from hardware (switches, routers, optical systems, radios), software and subscriptions, and support and services. Cisco's non-GAAP gross margin was 66.3% in its July 2026 quarter, with services at 71.6% against 64.8% for products [1]. Motorola Solutions splits sales between Products and Systems Integration and Software and Services [6].

Customers fall into four groups: hyperscalers and AI cloud builders, telecom carriers, enterprises and public-sector bodies, and consumers or small businesses. Cisco's fiscal 2026 hyperscale AI orders were $9.3 billion [2]. Nokia's AI and Cloud customers were about 12.2% of its revenue in Q3 2026 [8], and Motorola sells to public safety [6].

The main costs are cost of goods (chips, memory, optics, contract manufacturing), research and development, and sales and support. Many vendors outsource assembly. Component price rises were cited as pressure on margins at Arista and Ericsson [4][9].

Pricing power rests on technology lead, software and installed base. Arista holds a non-GAAP gross margin near 64% despite large cloud customers [3], while Nokia is deliberately shrinking low-margin Fixed Networks, down 21% [8]. Customers with large volumes negotiate terms [4].

Key assets are cash, inventory, receivables, intellectual property and acquired intangibles. Arista held about $14.4 billion of cash and marketable securities and $6.8 billion of deferred revenue at 30 September 2026 [3]. Ciena held $2.45 billion of cash [5]. Deferred revenue is a liability that represents future deliveries.

The group is mostly asset-light: design is in-house and assembly is outsourced. Ciena's nine-month equipment purchases were $194.9 million against $683.6 million of operating cash flow [5]. R&D and acquisitions, such as HPE's purchase of Juniper [7], are the larger commitments.
overview: No single figure covers the whole sub-industry, and we did not find one. Pieces are sized: Dell'Oro expects cumulative AI back-end switch spending to approach $1 trillion over 2026-2030 [11], while Ericsson describes the RAN market as flat [9]. So growth is split between a fast AI segment and a stable telecom one.

Main segments are data-centre networking, campus and enterprise networking, optical transport, mobile network equipment, and public-safety communications. Cisco competes across several [19]; Arista concentrates on data centres [3]; Ciena on optical [5]; Ericsson and Nokia on mobile and, for Nokia, IP and optical [8][9]; Motorola on mission-critical radios [6].

These companies sit between component suppliers (switch chips, memory, optical parts) and buyers such as clouds, carriers and governments. Ericsson says higher component costs will weigh on its 2027 gross margin [9]. Cloud buyers have bargaining power because they place very large orders [4].

The sub-industry has moved from carrier-led telecom hardware toward cloud and AI. Dell'Oro says AI back-end switch sales passed front-end sales for the first time in Q2 2026 and Ethernet has extended its lead [10]. Consolidation continues, with HPE integrating Juniper [7].

Customers are global. Nokia's Q3 2026 sales were EUR 2.152 billion in EMEA, EUR 1.833 billion in the Americas and EUR 1.169 billion in Asia-Pacific [8]. Cisco reports Americas, EMEA and APJC segments and had about 82,400 employees [19]. Much manufacturing is outsourced, so we cannot give a production split.
competition: There are a handful of significant competitors in each niche and many smaller ones. Cisco's filing names Arista, Broadcom, Ciena, Dell, HPE, Huawei, Nokia and Nvidia, among others, and says the list is not exhaustive [19].

In Ethernet AI back-end switching, Dell'Oro ranks Celestica first, Nvidia a close second, Arista third and Cisco fourth with the largest share gain of any vendor in Q2 2026 [10]. We did not find sourced shares for the whole sub-industry or for optical or RAN.

Concentration varies. AI switching is contested by a few large names plus white-box makers [10]. Mobile equipment is led by Ericsson and Nokia, with Huawei also named as a rival to Cisco [19]. Campus networking is more fragmented, with Cisco, HPE-Juniper and Ubiquiti among the names [7].

Barriers to entry are high: switch silicon, networking software, optical engineering and carrier or cloud qualification take years. Design wins matter; Nokia's AI and Cloud orders were EUR 1.5 billion in Q3 2026, up 118% [8].

Scale helps in R&D, supply access and channel reach. Cisco's 82,400 employees and global channel give breadth [19], and in tight supply, large buyers and vendors get components first. Dell'Oro expects supply to shape competition [10].

Products are differentiated at the high end (software, silicon, coherent optics) and more commoditised at the low end, such as fixed access, which Nokia is deliberately shrinking, with Fixed Networks sales down 21% [8]. Open Ethernet standards reduce lock-in in AI clusters [11].

Customers hold the power in cloud deals: Arista flags dependence on major cloud operators whose negotiating power can weigh on profitability [4]. Suppliers have power too: Ericsson expects higher component costs [9], and Dell'Oro notes the market is supply-constrained [10]. Ciena's top two customers were 41.7% of revenue [5].
drivers: Revenue growth follows hyperscaler capex, carrier budgets, enterprise refresh and public-safety spending. Five large spenders are forecast to spend $803-828 billion in 2026 [12], and Arista's revenue rose 58.5% in Q3 [3], against a flat RAN market [9].

Operating margin depends on mix, software share, volume leverage and component costs. Arista's non-GAAP operating margin was 49.1% [3], Cisco's 35.9% [1], Motorola's 32.5% [6], Ciena's 22.5% [5] and HPE Networking's 22.0% [7], which shows the spread by business model.

Key cost variables are memory, switch chips and optics, contract-manufacturing fees, tariffs, and engineering talent. Arista's gross margin fell 1.2 points year over year on mix, component pricing and customer terms [4]. Ericsson expects component costs to weigh on 2027 [9].

Interest-rate sensitivity is indirect: low leverage means little direct effect, but carrier and enterprise capex budgets and the cost of cloud-builder financing respond to rates. Damodaran's data show market debt to capital of just 8.47% for 57 telecom-equipment firms [16]. We did not find a source quantifying the rate effect.

Inflation matters through component and labour costs, and GDP and employment through enterprise and government spending. We found no sourced sensitivity to commodities. Cisco's guide of $72.2-73.4 billion for fiscal 2027 [1] and Motorola's raised full-year outlook [6] show the group absorbing a firm demand backdrop.

The group is a mix: AI networking is secular growth, carrier equipment is cyclical and flat now [9], and public-safety and support revenue is defensive. Motorola's backlog was a record $16.6 billion [6]. Cloud spending can still pause, so we would call AI a growth theme with cyclical risk.
financials: Growth is currently strong at the AI-exposed names: Cisco's fiscal 2026 revenue was up 12% to $63.3 billion [2], Arista's Q3 up 58.5% [3], Ciena's up 37% [5], Nokia's up 10% [8], Ericsson's organic up 7% [9]. S&P 500 blended Q3 earnings growth was 30.2% [17]; we found no sub-industry consensus.
Non-GAAP gross margins range from 46.4% at Ciena [5] to 64.0% at Arista [3] and 66.3% at Cisco [1]. Ericsson's was 47.7% adjusted [9]. HPE Networking reported 22.0% segment operating margin [7].

Damodaran's January 2026 table for 57 Telecom. Equipment firms shows an after-tax operating margin of 20.53%, versus 11.88% for the total market [13]. Company non-GAAP operating margins run from 22.5% to 49.1% [5][3].

Damodaran reports a return on invested capital of 52.73% for the industry, against 9.76% for the total market, with sales to invested capital of 2.57 [13]. We would treat that as flattered by the sample, since it is a January 2026 aggregate of US-listed firms, not a through-cycle figure.

Leverage is low: Damodaran shows market debt to capital of 8.47%, debt to EBITDA of 2.36 and interest coverage of 7.00 [16]. Ericsson had net cash of SEK 60.7 billion [9] and Nokia net cash of EUR 2.584 billion [8].

Free cash flow is strong at the large names but lumpy. Cisco generated $14.2 billion of operating cash flow in fiscal 2026, flat year on year [1]. Motorola's Q3 free cash flow was $589 million versus $733 million a year before [6]. Nokia's was negative EUR 99 million [8].

Damodaran's January 2026 data put forward P/E at 39.47 for Telecom. Equipment versus 27.66 for the total market, and EV/EBITDA at 24.07 versus 19.73 for positive-EBITDA firms [14][15]. S&P 500 forward P/E was 18.7 on 30 October 2026 [17].
risks: Regulation touches several areas: AI, privacy and cybersecurity rules are cited among Cisco's risks [19], and we found no source on export-control or tariff effects for the sub-industry. Telecom spectrum and security rules shape carrier demand, which we could not source.

AI is the main growth driver, but technology shifts can reshuffle winners. Dell'Oro sees Ethernet gaining against Nvidia's InfiniBand and NVLink in scale-up [11], and 1.6 Tbps switches ramping at least five times faster than 800 Gbps [11]. Vendors that miss a transition lose share.

Demographics matter little directly. Population and workforce trends influence carrier subscriber growth and public-safety budgets only slowly. We found no sourced evidence of a demographic effect on this sub-industry.

Consumer and enterprise behaviour shows in Wi-Fi and campus refresh: Cisco said Wi-Fi 7 was over 50% of wireless orders in Q4 [2]. Carriers' data demand growth has not turned into higher RAN spending, with the market flat [9].

New competitors and business models include white-box switch makers, Nvidia's networking, and silicon vendors. Dell'Oro lists Celestica and Nvidia ahead of Arista in Ethernet AI back-end sales [10]. Cisco's rise to fourth shows share can move quickly [10].

Geopolitics and supply chains are important: Dell'Oro expects supply constraints for one to two years [10], and Ericsson flags rising component costs [9]. Cisco's filing cites international and geopolitical risks [19]. Customer concentration at Ciena makes loss of a top buyer significant [5].

Substitutes include in-house cloud networking by hyperscalers and cheaper alternatives to carrier-grade equipment. Meta, Microsoft and others partner on Arista's Etherlink SU-144 design [4], showing customers shape products. We found no source sizing substitution risk.

opportunities: AI back-end switch spending is forecast to approach $1 trillion cumulatively over 2026-2030, with scale-up above half of the market by 2030 [11].
Nokia's IP Networks sales grew 45% and Optical 19% in Q3 2026 on AI and cloud demand [8].
Cisco guides to $72.2-73.4 billion of fiscal 2027 revenue, up from $63.3 billion [1][2].
Alphabet and Amazon both said they expect higher capex in 2027 [12].
threats: Hyperscaler budgets may flatten; Microsoft lowered its 2026 forecast on third-party data-centre delays [12].
Rising component costs and mix dilute gross margins, as flagged by Arista and Ericsson [4][9].
Concentrated customers can cut orders quickly: two customers were 41.7% of Ciena's revenue [5].
Mobile equipment stays flat, limiting growth at Ericsson [9].
horizon.assessment: Over three to five years, we think the sub-industry's results are set by whether the AI networking build continues at the pace implied by Dell'Oro's forecast [11] and hyperscaler guidance [12]. The evidence for the next year or two is strong: orders, backlogs and guidance are rising, and supply, not demand, is the limit [10]. The risks are about margin and durability. Mix and component costs are already trimming gross margins [3][9], valuation data from January 2026 sit well above the market [14], and the AI exposure is concentrated in a few buyers [5][12]. Carrier equipment is likely to remain a slow, flat business [9], with Motorola's public-safety backlog providing steadier growth [6]. Our read is that growth stays high while margins plateau, rather than a collapse or an unbroken climb.

paragraphs: This sub-industry is moving with a capex cycle rather than the consumer economy. The S&P 500 is in a strong earnings period, with blended third-quarter earnings growth of 30.2% and revenue growth of 13.4% as of 30 October 2026 [17]. The forward P/E of 18.7 is below its five-year average of 19.8 [17]. Within that, the key variable for equipment makers is spending by five large cloud and AI builders, forecast at $803-828 billion for 2026 and rising from $188.5 billion in Q2 to about $227 billion in Q3 [12].

Not all of the group rides that cycle. Ericsson describes the RAN market as flat and expects component costs to weigh on 2027 gross margin [9]. Nokia keeps its 2026 comparable operating profit target of EUR 2.1-2.6 billion while its Fixed Networks sales fell 21% and AI and Cloud sales rose 126% [8]. Public-safety demand shows up in Motorola's record $16.6 billion backlog [6]. We did not find a source tying interest rates or currency to this sub-industry's results, so we do not make a claim there. Our read is that the cycle is late-expansion for AI networking and flat for telecom.

The structural driver is AI. Dell'Oro's July 2026 forecast has cumulative AI back-end switch spending approaching $1 trillion over 2026-2030, with scale-up networking more than half of the market by 2030 and 1.6 Tbps ramping at least five times faster than 800 Gbps [11]. In Q2 2026, AI back-end switch sales passed front-end switch sales for the first time [10]. Cisco's hyperscale AI orders were $9.3 billion in fiscal 2026, about 4.5 times fiscal 2025 [2].

Demand is cyclical because it depends on a few buyers. The combined 2026 capex forecast is $803-828 billion, and Alphabet and Amazon said they expect to spend more in 2027, while Meta's plans are still being drawn up and Microsoft cut its 2026 estimate on data-centre delays [12]. Nokia's IP Networks grew 45% and Optical 19% in Q3 2026 [8]. Outside AI, demand is steadier: carrier RAN is flat [9], while enterprise Wi-Fi refresh is helped by Wi-Fi 7, over half of Cisco's Q4 wireless orders [2]. Demographics matter little here.

Porter's five forces point to a sub-industry with strong rivalry but high barriers. Threat of new entrants is low in carrier-grade and data-centre gear because silicon, software and customer qualification take years, but new-model entrants matter: Dell'Oro ranks Celestica first and Nvidia second in Ethernet AI back-end switching, ahead of Arista third and Cisco fourth, which made the biggest share gain [10]. Rivalry is intense; Cisco's filing names Arista, Broadcom, Ciena, Dell, HPE, Huawei, Nokia and Nvidia as competitors [19].

Buyer power is high: Arista's dependence on large clouds and their negotiating power is a flagged risk [4], and two customers were 41.7% of Ciena's revenue [5]. Supplier power is rising as memory, chips and optics tighten; Dell'Oro expects supply constraints for one to two years [10] and Ericsson sees higher component costs in 2027 [9]. The threat of substitutes comes from hyperscalers' own designs and Nvidia's proprietary links; Dell'Oro expects Ethernet to become the leading scale-up technology by 2030 [11]. Moats are software (Arista's EOS), silicon (Cisco Silicon One) and installed base; the sourced evidence is margin: Arista 64.0% gross [3], Cisco 66.3% [1].

Political and regulatory factors we could source are limited. Cisco's 10-K lists regulation of AI, privacy and cybersecurity, international and geopolitical conditions and currency among its risk factors [19]. We did not locate current sources on export controls, tariffs or telecom spectrum policy for this group, so we make no claim about them.

Technology is the largest force. Ethernet has extended its lead in AI back-end networks, 800 Gbps switches account for most Ethernet AI back-end revenue and 1.6 Tbps switches have begun sampling [10]. Scale-up networking, currently dominated by Nvidia's NVLink, is expected to open to Ethernet and UALink [11]. Cisco shipped more than 75,000 800G coherent pluggables in fiscal 2026 and says three hyperscalers use its P200 platform for scale-across networks [2]. Arista introduced its Etherlink SU-144 design in October [4]. Economic factors include component and memory availability [4][9]. Social and environmental factors, such as power use of AI sites, were not covered by sources we opened.

Margins differ widely by business model. Non-GAAP operating margin was 49.1% at Arista [3], 35.9% at Cisco in its July 2026 quarter [1], 32.5% at Motorola Solutions [6], 22.5% at Ciena [5] and 22.0% for HPE Networking [7]. Ericsson's adjusted EBITA margin was 17.0%, down from 28.1% a year before, which included a large capital gain [9]. Nokia's comparable operating margin was 11.7% [8]. Damodaran's January 2026 industry table shows a 20.53% after-tax operating margin and 52.73% return on invested capital for 57 telecom-equipment firms, against 11.88% and 9.76% for the market [13].

Gross-margin direction is mixed. Ciena's non-GAAP gross margin rose to 46.4% from 41.9% [5] while Cisco's non-GAAP fell to 66.3% from 68.4% [1], Arista's to 64.0% from 65.2% [3] and Ericsson's adjusted gross margin was 47.7% versus 48.1% [9]. Balance sheets are strong: Arista has about $14.4 billion in cash and securities [3], Ericsson net cash of SEK 60.7 billion [9]. Cisco's fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was $14.2 billion, flat [1]. Capital intensity is low, as Ciena's nine-month equipment purchases were $194.9 million [5].

Company guidance is the best evidence we have; we did not find sub-industry consensus estimates. FactSet's S&P 500 data show Q4 2026 earnings growth expected at 28.4% and calendar 2026 at 32.9%, but it gives no figure for this sub-industry [17]. Cisco guides fiscal 2027 revenue to $72.2-73.4 billion and non-GAAP EPS to $5.05-5.11, against $4.33 in fiscal 2026 [1]. Arista guides Q4 revenue to $3.9-4.0 billion with a 48-49% non-GAAP operating margin and EPS of $1.26-1.30 [3]. Ciena guides fiscal 2026 revenue to $6.42 billion and Q4 to $1.75 billion [5]. Motorola raised full-year non-GAAP EPS to $17.94-17.99 [6]. Nokia sees Q4 revenue up 20-24% sequentially and 2026 comparable operating profit of EUR 2.1-2.6 billion [8].

Our read is that the revisions are positive for AI networking: Arista's Q4 guide was above the roughly $3.6 billion analysts expected [4], and Nokia's AI and Cloud orders rose 118% [8]. The difference from a simple extrapolation is gross margin, where mix and component costs are working against growth [3][4][9]. Ericsson's flat RAN outlook [9] is the main drag in the group.

We have no sourced current multiple for the sub-industry. The best reference is Damodaran's January 2026 dataset, now ten months old, which shows a forward P/E of 39.47 for 57 Telecom. Equipment firms against 27.66 for the total market, a trailing P/E of 84.72, and a PEG ratio of 0.87 against 1.90 [14]. On enterprise value, EV/EBITDA is 24.07 versus 19.73 for the market for positive-EBITDA firms, and EV/EBIT is 30.86 versus 29.12 [15]. The S&P 500 forward P/E was 18.7 on 30 October 2026, under its five-year average of 19.8 [17].

Read together, we think the group was priced at a premium to the market on earnings but nearer parity on a growth-adjusted basis in January, which fits the PEG ratio [14]. Since then, estimates for AI networking names have moved up, and Arista's shares were about 25% below their all-time high at about $180 after its November results [4]. We did not find a current free-cash-flow yield for the group, and these January figures should be treated as stale for individual stocks.

We found no sourced short-interest, fund-flow or breadth data for this sub-industry, so this section is limited to what the opened ETF page shows. The iShares U.S. Telecommunications ETF (IYZ), which holds communications-equipment names alongside carriers, had $701 million of assets and 26 holdings in its page updated 5 November 2026. Its top weights were Cisco at 22.90%, Verizon 12.32%, Arista 10.63%, AT&T 4.54% and Motorola Solutions 4.52%, with the top ten at 73.02% [18]. That shows how concentrated exposure to this group is in a handful of names.

Price momentum is mixed in what we saw. Arista rose about 6% after its results but closed below its 200-day average and about 25% below its all-time high, per XTB [4]. Hyperscaler capex data and Dell'Oro's supply-constraint view [10][12] argue that fundamentals are still ahead of positioning, but we cannot back that with flow data. Readers should check current ETF holdings and prices before relying on any weight here.
